content: The enzyme known as polyphosphoinositide phosphatase, also referred to as phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate 5-phosphatase or SAC domain-containing protein 3 (Sac3), is encoded by the FIG4 gene in humans. The abbreviation FIG4 stands for Factor-Induced Gene. The Sac3 protein is part of a family of human phosphoinositide phosphatases that contain a Sac1-homology domain. This domain spans approximately 400 amino acids and includes seven conserved motifs, which feature the catalytic sequence CX5R(T/S) that is also present in other lipid and protein tyrosine phosphatases. The founding protein containing this evolutionarily conserved domain was first identified in a screen for suppressors of yeast actin mutations and was named Sac1. In humans, there are five genes containing a Sac1 domain. Three of these genes (SACM1L, INPP5F, and FIG4) have a single Sac1 domain, while the other two genes, synaptojanin 1 and 2, have a Sac1 domain coexisting with another phosphoinositide phosphatase domain, both of which contribute to phosphate hydrolysis. The human Sac3 cDNA, which encodes a 907-amino acid protein, was first reported in 1996 and is localized to chromosome 6. Sac3 is a widely expressed 97-kDa protein that exhibits in vitro phosphatase activity toward various 5’-phosphorylated phosphoinositides. Sac3 forms a hetero-oligomeric complex with ArPIKfyve (encoded by the VAC14 gene), and this binary complex associates with the phosphoinositide kinase PIKfyve to form a ternary PAS complex (PIKfyve-ArPIKfyve-Sac3). This complex is essential for maintaining proper endosomal membrane dynamics. The physical association of two enzymes with opposing functions within this complex leads to the activation of PIKfyve and an increase in PtdIns(3,5)P2 production. Sac3 is active within the triple complex and is responsible for converting PtdIns(3,5)P2 to PtdIns3P. The PAS complex is critical for survival, as knockout of any of the three genes encoding PIKfyve, ArPIKfyve, or Sac3 results in early embryonic, perinatal, or early juvenile lethality in mice. Sac3 protein has a very short half-life of approximately 18 minutes due to rapid proteasomal degradation. However, co-expression of ArPIKfyve significantly prolongs Sac3’s half-life, while siRNA-mediated knockdown of ArPIKfyve drastically reduces Sac3 levels. The cellular levels of Sac3 are critically dependent on its physical interaction with ArPIKfyve, and the C-terminal region of Sac3 is essential for this interaction. Insulin treatment of 3T3-L1 adipocytes inhibits Sac3 phosphatase activity in vitro. A partial knockdown (~60%) of endogenous Sac3 using small interfering RNA (siRNA) results in a slight but significant increase in PtdIns(3,5)P2 levels in 3T3-L1 adipocytes, which enhances GLUT4 translocation and glucose uptake in response to insulin. Conversely, ectopic expression of Sac3, but not a phosphatase-deficient mutant, reduces GLUT4 plasma membrane abundance in response to insulin. Thus, Sac3 is an insulin-sensitive lipid phosphatase, and its downregulation improves insulin responsiveness. Mutations in the FIG4 gene are associated with the rare autosomal recessive Charcot-Marie-Tooth peripheral neuropathy type 4J (CMT4J). FIG4 mutations have also been identified in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), although causation has not been definitively established. In CMT4J, one FIG4 allele is null, while the other encodes a mutant protein with a threonine-to-isoleucine substitution at position 41 (I41T). The Sac3 I41T mutation disrupts the protective effect of ArPIKfyve on Sac3’s half-life, although the interaction between the two proteins is largely preserved. As a result, Sac3 I41T protein levels in patient fibroblasts are very low due to proteasomal degradation. Clinically, the onset and severity of CMT4J symptoms vary significantly, suggesting that genetic background plays a critical role in the disease course. In two siblings with severe peripheral motor deficits and moderate sensory symptoms, the disease had relatively little impact on the central nervous system. The mechanism by which a molecular defect affecting all cells results in selective peripheral neuropathy remains unknown. In mouse models, spontaneous FIG4 knockout results in smaller-sized mice with selectively reduced PtdIns(3,5)P2 levels in fibroblasts, diluted pigmentation, central and peripheral neurodegeneration, hydrocephalus, abnormal tremor and gait, and eventual juvenile lethality. These mice are referred to as pale tremor mice (plt). Neuronal autophagy has been proposed as a significant consequence of the knockout, although its primary relevance is debated. The plt mice exhibit distinct morphological defects in motor and central neurons, as well as sensory neurons. The phenotypes of plt mice, which are considered the genotypic equivalent of human CMT4J, can be dose-dependently rescued from lethality, neurodegeneration, and brain apoptosis by genetic interventions. However, hydrocephalus and diluted pigmentation are not corrected. From an evolutionary perspective, genes encoding orthologs of human Sac3 are present in all eukaryotes. The most studied ortholog is the Saccharomyces cerevisiae gene FIG4, which was discovered in a screen for yeast pheromone (Factor)-Induced Genes, hence the name FIG, with the number 4 reflecting the order of its isolation. Yeast Fig4p is a specific PtdIns(3,5)P2 5’-phosphatase that physically interacts with Vac14p (the ortholog of human ArPIKfyve) and the PtdIns(3,5)P2-producing enzyme Fab1p (the ortholog of PIKfyve). The yeast Fab1p-Vac14p-Fig4p complex also involves Vac7p and potentially Atg18p. Deletion of Fig4p in budding yeast has relatively minor effects on growth, basal PtdIns(3,5)P2 levels, and vacuolar size compared to deletions of Vac14p or Fab1p. In summary, Sac3/Fig4 has retained the Sac1 domain, phosphoinositide phosphatase activity, and protein interactions from yeast through evolution. In mice, the protein is essential for early postnatal development, while in humans, the I41T point mutation combined with a null allele causes a neurodegenerative disorder.
